The record:
Write the overview of the executive synopsis for the incident on io-shop below: a short paragraph in plain words, for the people who lead the company rather than the engineers who responded - what happened, how long it lasted, what it cost the business and the people who responded, and how it was resolved.

What a reader saw: Shop requests slowed down for shoppers
Why, in plain words: The shop's memory kept filling up until the shop slowed down, most likely because it kept a note of every shopper who opened their account page and only cleared those notes when it was restarted.

Figures:
- How long it lasted: 39m 52s {duration}
- What it cost the shop in takings (estimated by Argus): none {customer_loss}
- Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.

What was done to end it:
- Argus: restarted io-shop - confirmed
- Argus: proposed a fix, PR #542 - opened as a draft

Name {duration} and {customer_loss} in your overview.
Write no figure yourself - not in digits, not spelled out, and not as a word that sizes it ("a brief outage", "a minor loss", "tripled"). Where a figure goes, write its name, braces and all, and the synopsis writes the figure in.
Say nothing about how the incident was resolved beyond what the list of what was done says: a draft fix has not run, and nothing it would do has happened.
Speak of Argus by name, never as "we", "our" or "us": Argus is the system that responded, and each line of what was done says who did it.
Where you say who was affected, say which ones, as the cause does, or that some were, where it does not say which - never how many, and never all of them, where the cause does not say all.
Keep "likely" on what the cause says is likely, and only there.

Call submit_executive_overview with your overview.

The postmortem it is written from:
Shop requests slowed down for shoppers
Incident: HighMemoryUsage on io-shop
Date: Nov 11, 2026, 02:34 to 03:13:52 UTC
Status: Draft. 1 of 6 action items are done.
Written by: Argus Postmortem agent, Nov 11, 2026, 03:32:53 UTC. Not reviewed yet. Each part is as of when the work it reports ended, which the timeline dates; who ended the incident is as of now.
First told: Argus posted in Slack, Nov 11, 2026, 03:13:19 UTC
Ended by: Argus: restarted io-shop - confirmed, nothing to put back

Summary
The service broke at 02:34 UTC and was back to normal at 03:13:52 UTC, 39 minutes 52 seconds later. Requests took longer: the median request went from 44.9 ms before it began to 297 ms at its worst, the slowest one request in twenty from 215 ms to 1449 ms, and the slowest one request in a hundred from 380 ms to 2412 ms. What its alert watches went from 21.7% before it began to 84.4% at its worst. The shop's takings fell short of the same hours on earlier weeks by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all. The shop's memory kept filling up until the shop slowed down, most likely because it kept a note of every shopper who opened their account page and only cleared those notes when it was restarted. What Argus did: restarted io-shop - confirmed, nothing to put back. Argus opened a draft fix, PR #542, for a person to review and merge. Until a fix is in place, the shop's memory can climb toward its limit again after the restart and slow requests the same way.

Impact
39m 52s - onset until back to normal
1.0% to 1.0% - error rate, before onset and while broken on average (no rise)
44.9 ms to 122 ms - p50 latency, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 297 ms)
215 ms to 586 ms - p95 latency, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 1449 ms)
380 ms to 1027 ms - p99 latency, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 2412 ms)
21.7% to 56.3% - what the alert watches, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 84.4%; the rule's line is 60%)
none - customer loss (estimated)

Root cause and contributing factors
serve_account_page calls record_visit on every account page render, on failure and on success (U1, U2), and according to Code-Fix's reading record_visit adds each new shopper to `_LAST_SEEN`, a module-level dict in `src/io_shop/visits.py` that nothing but `forget_every_visit()` empties. That means the process's resident memory keeps growing with every new shopper until a restart, and requests slow down as it nears the container limit. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
Causal chain
symptom Shoppers' requests to io-shop took longer from the onset, and the slowest requests slowed down the most.
  Evidence:
    T4 03:13:40 Investigator Agent: Read back 361 minutes of metrics
    T5 03:13:41 Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 02:34
why 1 Requests slowed while the io-shop process's resident memory climbed steadily toward its container limit.
  Evidence:
    AL1 Memory usage climbing against the container limit for 15m
    T4
why 2 The memory built up inside the running process, not because of a change to production: no deploy or flag change was found, and restarting io-shop brought the service back down from the incident's level.
  Evidence:
    T8 03:13:44 Investigator Agent: Read back 0 production changes
    T13 03:13:46 Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 03:13:45
    T15 03:13:52 Mitigation Agent: Restarted io-shop for C1
    T17 03:15:16 Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 03:13
    T18 03:15:16 Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
  Ruled out:
    A deploy, release or flag change on the service: the Investigator Agent asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 11 02:35; the Investigator Agent read back 0 production changes.
      T7
      T8
    A flag change by anyone but Argus: Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 03:13:45.
      T13
why 3 Memory grew with every new shopper served an account page: serve_account_page calls record_visit on every render, on failure and on success, and according to Code-Fix's reading record_visit adds the shopper to a module-level store that only a restart empties.
  Evidence:
    U1 record_visit at src/io_shop/account_page.py:156, in serve_account_page: calls it: record_visit(account.shopper_id, failure)
    U2 record_visit at src/io_shop/account_page.py:160, in serve_account_page: calls it: record_visit(account.shopper_id, str(figure_cents))
    F1 What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
Contributing factors
- The slowdown was found only by the memory alert, which waits for its condition to hold before it fires. No alert on io-shop request latency, or on how fast memory was growing toward the limit, was seen firing. (AI-3, AI-4)
- No check was seen that runs io-shop against many different shoppers for a long time and watches whether its memory keeps growing before code is released. (AI-5)

Hypotheses considered
 | Hypothesis | Confidence | Result
C1 | io-shop's memory grew steadily from about 02:30 UTC, from roughly 465MB to 1.8GB of the 2GB limit, with no matching increase in traffic. No deploy or flag change accompanied it. Latency then degraded as memory pressure built, starting around 02:49 UTC. This fits a leak inside the running process. The evidence doesn't show which allocation is leaking. | 0.80 | confirmed
C2 | Demand saturation is a less likely alternative. Traffic is flat at 1200 requests per minute, which argues against it. | 0.08 | never tried

Trigger
C1 was confirmed, but it names nothing specific, so no change could be matched to it.

Resolution
 | Time (UTC) | Action | By | Kind | Outcome
M1 | 03:13:52 | Restarted io-shop for C1 | Argus | nothing to put back | confirmed
 | 03:17:02 | Proposed a fix: PR #542 | Code-Fix Agent | nothing to put back | opened as a draft

Detection
The incident on io-shop began at 02:34 UTC. HighMemoryUsage fired at 03:12:54 UTC, 38 minutes 54 seconds later.
What the alert said
AL1 | Memory usage climbing against the container limit for 15m

Action items
Item | Action | Type | Owner | Tracking | Status
AI-1 | Restarted io-shop | mitigate | Argus | - | done
AI-2 | Review and merge the proposed fix | prevent | unassigned | PR #542 | open
AI-3 | Add an alert on io-shop request latency at the slow percentiles, compared with its normal level. | detect | unassigned | - | open
AI-4 | Add an alert that fires when io-shop's resident memory is on course to reach its container limit, based on its growth trend. | detect | unassigned | - | open
AI-5 | Add a soak test to the release pipeline that renders account pages for a large number of different shoppers and fails if the process's resident memory keeps growing. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-6 | Route HighMemoryUsage on io-shop to the on-call paging rotation so that a person is paged when it fires. | process | unassigned | - | open

Lessons learned
What went well
- The alert came 16 minutes 54 seconds after its series passed its line, within the 17 minutes 30 seconds accounted for by its rule waiting 15 minutes with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
- 58 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent restarted io-shop for C1.
- 2 minutes 22 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent judged the action CONFIRMED.
- 52 seconds after the alert was raised, Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 03:13:45.
- 4 minutes 8 seconds after the alert was raised, the Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #542.
What went wrong
- Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to the alert, so no person was brought in.
Where it got lucky
Nothing.

Timeline (UTC)
 | Nov 11 02:34 | IMPACT BEGINS | the incident began
 | 03:12:54 | DETECTED | HighMemoryUsage on io-shop fired
T1 | 03:13:15 |  | Argus Received HighMemoryUsage on io-shop
T2 | 03:13:27 |  | Argus Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
T3 | 03:13:35 |  | Investigator Agent Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 03:12:54
T4 | 03:13:40 |  | Investigator Agent Read back 361 minutes of metrics
T5 | 03:13:41 |  | Investigator Agent Placed the start of the incident at 02:34
T6 | 03:13:42 |  | Investigator Agent Recorded where the 3 replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
T7 | 03:13:43 |  | Investigator Agent Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 11 02:35
T8 | 03:13:44 |  | Investigator Agent Read back 0 production changes
T9 | 03:13:44 |  | Investigator Agent Asked for the service's log lines, the 20 minutes before 02:46
T10 | 03:13:44 |  | Investigator Agent Read back 53 log lines
T11 | 03:13:45 |  | Investigator Agent Formed 2 candidate causes, best first: C1, C2
T12 | 03:13:45 |  | Investigator Agent Read every channel available
T13 | 03:13:46 |  | Argus Read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 03:13:45
T14 | 03:13:50 |  | Argus Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate
T15 | 03:13:52 | MITIGATION APPLIED | Mitigation Agent Restarted io-shop for C1

T16 | 03:14 |  | Mitigation Agent Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 03:14 - up to 127s
T17 | 03:15:16 |  | Mitigation Agent Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 03:13
T18 | 03:15:16 |  | Mitigation Agent Judged the action CONFIRMED
T19 | 03:15:16 |  | Argus Moved the incident to MITIGATED - restarted io-shop and the rule that fired stopped firing
T20 | 03:17:02 |  | Code-Fix Agent Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #542

Response effort
none - engineer time
175,384 - tokens spent by Argus

Supporting information
The incident's walk: http://localhost:8000/incidents/2b3db416-5487-4a49-9109-0af3e2d9a000
The fix it proposed: PR #542 (https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/542) opened as a draft. The record holds nothing about it after that.
Changes to production read
Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.
Log messages read (UTC)
G46bc | ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 32 occurrences in 21 minutes, 02:26–02:46
Gbac1 | WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 20 occurrences in 21 minutes, 02:26–02:46; # was 0.50% to 3.00%, typically 1.00%, highest at 02:31
Gad41 | INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 1 occurrence in 1 minute, 02:43
What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
F1 | The fault: src/io_shop/visits.py keeps _LAST_SEEN, a module-level dict keyed by shopper id. serve_account_page in src/io_shop/account_page.py calls record_visit on every render, both on success and in its exception handler. The only thing that removes entries is forget_every_visit(). So the dict grows by one entry for each new shopper and is only emptied on a restart. Its own docstring says it "holds whichever of them have been by", out of a few million shoppers. That matches memory rising steadily without more traffic, with no deploy and no restart. The investigation didn't name the allocation; this is the only unbounded process-level store I found that the request path writes to.

The fix: _LAST_SEEN is now an OrderedDict used as a least-recently-used cache, capped at MOST_SHOPPERS_REMEMBERED (100,000) entries. record_visit moves the shopper to the newest end and, if the store is over the cap, drops the oldest entries. what_they_saw_last_time also marks a found shopper as recently used. If a shopper has been evicted, the lookup returns None, which callers already handle for a first-time visitor. So the cost of eviction is an empty panel while the figure loads, the same as for a new shopper. The function names and signatures are unchanged, so account_page.py and the existing tests need no changes.

Tests added to tests/io_shop/test_visits.py:
• Recording more shoppers than the cap leaves exactly the cap. The current code would hold all of them, so this test is written to fail against it.
• The oldest shopper is the one evicted, and the newest are kept.
• A shopper who visits again, or whose last figure is read, is kept over one who hasn't been seen since.
How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main
U1 | record_visit at src/io_shop/account_page.py:156, in serve_account_page: calls it: record_visit(account.shopper_id, failure)
U2 | record_visit at src/io_shop/account_page.py:160, in serve_account_page: calls it: record_visit(account.shopper_id, str(figure_cents))
Assumptions
- Exchange rate: EUR converted at 0.92191 per USD, published 2026-11-10
- No engineer minutes: no on-call incident was linked to this one, so nobody was paged to respond

Review checklist
✓ Key incident data collected (met)
✓ Impact assessed (met)
○ Root-cause analysis complete (for a person)
  running the proposed fix's tests against the current code would confirm the reading, not that the code it reads is what ran (AI-2)
○ Every action item owned and dated (for a person)
○ Reviewed and shared (for a person)

The document, by field:
overview: The io-shop online shop slowed down for some shoppers for {duration}. The shop's memory kept filling up until it slowed. This was most likely because the shop kept a note of every shopper who opened their account page and only cleared those notes when it was restarted. Argus estimates the lost takings at {customer_loss}. Nobody was paged, and no on-call incident was linked to this one. Argus restarted io-shop, and the restart was confirmed. Argus also proposed a fix, which is still a draft. It hasn't been put into use yet and has changed nothing so far.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {duration}, are figures code writes in from the list of figures in the ask. They are not judged.
  - The overview is written in plain words for the people who lead the company. A claim said more plainly than the postmortem says it is grounded where it means the same.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
